messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 56

He is twenty-eight years old, and he spends most of his day staring at a screen that doesn’t feel like a screen. It feels like a window he can’t close, a feed that won’t stop feeding him images he never asked for. He works as a social media manager for a mid-sized outdoor gear company, which means his job is to curate optimism—sunlit trails, smiling hikers, clean tents pitched beside calm lakes. He is good at it. He knows the algorithms, the right hashtags, the cadence of a caption that makes people stop scrolling. But the scrolling itself is the problem. Every time he opens Instagram or Twitter, he is waiting for the wrong image to appear. A dust cloud. A twisted piece of metal. A face he used to know.

The trauma happened three years ago, during his second deployment to Afghanistan. He was a vehicle operator in a logistics convoy, driving supply trucks between forward operating bases. That day, the route had been quiet, which made everyone nervous. He remembers the heat pressing through the armored cab, the taste of dust and diesel, the way the radio crackled with static. Then the blast. An IED buried in the road, detonated under the lead vehicle. He didn’t see the explosion—he was two trucks back—but he heard it, felt it in his chest, and then he saw the smoke and the fire and the pieces of things that used to be whole. They pulled the driver out, or what was left of him. The man’s name was Corporal Reyes. He had a wife back home and a baby girl he’d only seen in photos. He had been twenty-two.

That night, and every night since, the images repeat themselves. He does not have full-blown flashbacks with visual hallucinations, but the memory is so vivid it might as well be happening. He feels the heat. He smells the burning fuel and something else, something organic. He hears the shouting and the crying. And then he feels nothing, which is worse—a numbing emptiness that slides over him like a shroud. He tells himself he should have been in the lead truck. He tells himself he could have done something. He knows, rationally, that is not true, but the thought sits inside him like a stone he cannot swallow.

When he came home, he tried to go back to his old life. He finished his degree in communications, found the social media job, moved in with his girlfriend, Olivia. She is patient. She is kind. But he cannot tell her what he sees when he closes his eyes. He cannot tell her why he flinches when a car backfires on the street, or why he sometimes cancels plans because the thought of a crowded bar makes his skin crawl. He avoids loud noises, crowds, even the news—anything that might trigger the memory. He has unfollowed every veteran’s page on social media. He has blocked all military-related hashtags. Still, the algorithm finds him. A video of a convoy in Ukraine. A photo of a soldier hugging his daughter. The image of a boot. He freezes, his heart pounds, his palms sweat, and then he closes the tab and opens a spreadsheet of hiking trail photos, and he tries to breathe.

At work, his boss praises his engagement metrics. He is always online. He is always responsive. But inside, he is hollow. He does not feel pride in his work. He feels like a machine performing a script. His relationship with Olivia is strained—he loves her, but he cannot be present. He lies awake next to her at night, scanning the dark for threats that are not there. He has not cried since the deployment. He has not felt joy in months. He simply exists, scrolling forward, waiting for the next blast.
